content: The following studies and guidelines provide detailed insights into the diagnosis, treatment, and management of cryptococcal meningitis, particularly in individuals living with HIV: 1. Rothman et al. conducted a placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of maintenance therapy with fluconazole following treatment for cryptococcal meningitis in patients with AIDS. This study was part of the California Collaborative Treatment Group and was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1991. 2. Saag et al. compared itraconazole and fluconazole as maintenance therapies for AIDS-associated cryptococcal meningitis. This study, conducted by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Mycoses Study Group, was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 1999. 3. Powderly et al. performed a controlled trial to assess the effectiveness of fluconazole versus amphotericin B in preventing relapse of cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS patients. This research, conducted by the NIAID AIDS Clinical Trials Group and Mycoses Study Group, was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1992. 4. Troncoso et al. reported a case of central nervous system cryptococcoma in an HIV-positive patient, highlighting the clinical presentation and management. This case was published in the Journal of the International Association of Physicians in AIDS Care in 2002. 5. Velamakanni et al. described a case of CNS cryptococcoma in a Ugandan patient with HIV, emphasizing the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. This case report was published in Medical Mycology Case Reports in 2014. 6. Klock et al. analyzed the histopathological aspects of neurocryptococcosis in HIV-infected patients through autopsy reports of 45 cases. This study was published in the International Journal of Surgical Pathology in 2009. 7. Dromer et al., as part of the French Cryptococcosis Study Group, investigated the determinants of disease presentation and outcomes during cryptococcosis in the CryptoA/D study. This research was published in PLoS Medicine in 2007. 8. Charlier et al. correlated radiological lesions with disease severity in HIV-positive patients with cryptococcal meningoencephalitis during the HAART era. This study was published in PLoS One in 2008. 9. Loyse et al. examined neurological, visual, and MRI findings in 87 South African patients with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningoencephalitis. This study was published in the Journal of Infection in 2015. 10. Zhang et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the safety of oral fluconazole during the first trimester of pregnancy. This study was published in BJOG in 2019. 11. Beardsley et al. investigated the use of adjunctive dexamethasone in HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. This study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2016. 12. Eshun-Wilson et al. compared early versus delayed antiretroviral therapy initiation in HIV-positive individuals with cryptococcal meningitis. This Cochrane systematic review was published in 2018. 13. Sun et al. This study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2004. 14. Meda et al. evaluated the management of cryptococcal meningitis in Tanzania using a strict schedule of serial lumbar punctures. This operational research study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2014. 15. Perfect et al. provided updated clinical practice guidelines for the management of cryptococcal disease, published by the Infectious Diseases Society of America in 2010. 16. Newton et al. This study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2002. 17. Haddow et al. proposed clinical case definitions for cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome in HIV-1-infected individuals. This study was published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2010. 18. Larson et al. assessed the cost-effectiveness of screening HIV-infected patients with low CD4 counts for cryptococcal antigenemia before initiating antiretroviral therapy in South Africa. This study was published in PLoS One in 2016. 19. Vallabhaneni et al. evaluated a public-sector cryptococcal antigen screening and treatment program in the Western Cape, South Africa. This operational research study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2016. 20. Rick et al. explored the feasibility of lay cadres conducting cryptococcal antigen screening using rapid tests in rural Lesotho. This study was published in PLoS One in 2017. 21. Loyse et al. highlighted the need to improve access to essential antifungal medicines for cryptococcal meningitis in resource-poor countries. This study was published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2013. 22. Smilnak et al. proposed a novel treatment for cryptococcal meningitis using neurapheresis therapy. This study was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2018. 23. WHO guidelines for diagnosing, preventing, and managing cryptococcal disease among adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV have been updated periodically, with significant revisions in 2018 and 2021. These updates reflect new evidence on induction therapy and other management strategies. 24. A systematic review led by Adrienne Shapiro at the University of Washington School of Medicine provided updated evidence on induction therapy for HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. This review informed the revision of WHO guidelines. 25. The WHO Guideline Development Group used the GRADE methodology to assess the certainty of evidence and formulate recommendations. This process included systematic reviews, cost-effectiveness analyses, and stakeholder consultations. 26. The AMBITION trial demonstrated that a single high-dose of liposomal amphotericin B combined with fluconazole and flucytosine is as effective as the standard seven-day amphotericin B regimen in reducing mortality from cryptococcal meningitis. This finding has significant implications for resource-limited settings. 27. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of screening for cryptococcal antigenemia in HIV-positive individuals with low CD4 counts and providing preemptive antifungal therapy to those who test positive. 28. 29. The development of these guidelines involved extensive peer review, conflict of interest management, and input from global experts in HIV and cryptococcal disease. 30. The WHO continues to prioritize improving access to antifungal medicines and implementing cost-effective strategies for managing cryptococcal meningitis in resource-limited settings.
